analysis.one_liner: Caps prices for 50 expensive drugs under Medicare and applies the negotiated prices to private insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended Medicare-negotiated drug prices to private insurance plans, never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the government negotiates maximum prices for a limited number of the most expensive brand-name drugs, but only for people on Medicare. This bill would raise the number of negotiated drugs from 20 to 50 and, for the first time, apply those negotiated prices to drugs covered by private health insurance (with insurers allowed to opt out, but only if they publicly disclose it). It would also extend the rule that drug companies pay rebates when their prices rise faster than inflation to drugs sold in the private market.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who take expensive brand-name drugs would pay less, because their plans would be required to charge cost-sharing based on the Medicare-negotiated price unless their insurer opts out. People on Medicare would also benefit, since more of the highest-cost drugs would be subject to negotiation. Anyone whose drug price has climbed faster than inflation would benefit from the rebate requirement being extended to the private market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Privately insured people taking expensive brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: Raises the number of drugs subject to Medicare price negotiation from 20 to 50 beginning in 2029.
Applies the Medicare-negotiated maximum price to drugs covered under private group and individual insurance plans, and caps the patient's cost-sharing at no more than that negotiated price.
Requires insurers that choose not to participate to publicly disclose that decision before the plan year begins, with the government publishing lists of opting-out insurers.
Extends the inflation rebate requirement — where manufacturers pay back money when drug prices rise faster than inflation — from Medicare to drugs sold in the private market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the main cost, since negotiated maximum prices and inflation rebates would apply to sales in the commercial market and not just Medicare. Health insurers would face new administrative obligations and, if they participate, would pass lower drug prices through to plans and members.

drawbacks.text: Participation by private insurers is voluntary: a plan or insurer can simply opt out of the negotiated prices, so the protection for privately insured patients depends on insurers choosing to join or on public pressure created by the disclosure lists rather than on a requirement.

Manufacturers warn that expanding price negotiation and inflation rebates to the commercial market reduces revenue from new medicines, which they argue could mean fewer drugs brought to market over time; this is the standard objection to government price-setting and is disputed.
The bill reaches only the selected drugs chosen for the program, so patients taking drugs not on the negotiated list would see no change in price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families facing high out-of-pocket costs on expensive brand-name drugs, the bill offers a real and direct benefit: the same price the government wins for Medicare patients would flow through to private plans, with a hard cap on cost-sharing. The opt-out design weakens that benefit — insurers can decline, and the bill's remedy is public disclosure rather than a mandate — so how much it helped would have depended partly on public shaming of insurers that walk away. The research-and-development objection is real but contested; the same tradeoff was accepted when the underlying Medicare negotiation program was enacted.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and its Health Subcommittee, and it sat there for the rest of the session — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on July 28, 2023, and referred again to that subcommittee on December 17, 2024, with no other action recorded.
The bill never received a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill was sponsored and cosponsored exclusively by House Democrats — the sponsor plus 74 of the 216 House Democrats — with no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off, because they keep charging commercial-market prices free of Medicare-negotiated caps and inflation rebates. Health insurers are also better off, since they face no federal negotiated prices and no obligation to disclose nonparticipation.

industries.note: The bill would extend Medicare-negotiated maximum prices and inflation rebates to drugs sold in the private market, cutting into revenue the industry currently earns from commercial sales. Blocking it preserves the status quo in which Americans with private insurance pay some of the highest drug prices in the world.

Participating plans would have to pass negotiated prices through to members and cap cost-sharing, but insurers could opt out entirely — the bill's only lever is public disclosure of that choice. Insurers gain from the outcome only insofar as they avoided the obligation.
